tagline.text: A July river festival where a pagoda barge carries the Holy Cross downstream

location.label: Location
location.text: Bocaue, Bulacan (along the Bocaue River and around St. Martin of Tours Parish Church)

children.text: The Bocaue Pagoda Festival is a river procession held in Bocaue, Bulacan, centered on the first Sunday of July each year. A brightly decorated barge called the pagoda carries the Holy Cross of Wawa down the Bocaue River while smaller boats circle and follow it.
The Bocaue Pagoda Festival is a Catholic devotional event held in Bocaue, Bulacan, around the first Sunday of July each year. It is also called the Bocaue River Festival, and it honors the town's
Holy Cross of Wawa (Mahal na Poon Krus sa Wawa)

. The heart of the festival is the procession on the river. A cross, or a replica of it, is placed on a large decorated barge called the pagoda, which glides slowly along the river while smaller boats surround it and follow.

According to tradition, this wooden cross was found floating in the Wawa area of the Bocaue River during a typhoon in 1850. The story goes that a drowning woman clung to the cross and was saved, and residents regard this as a miracle. The timber is believed to come from an older church that burned down, and the cross is now enshrined at St. Martin of Tours Parish Church in Bocaue. The custom of enshrining it in a riverside church and honoring it with a river procession is said to have grown into today's festival.

No account of this festival is complete without the tragedy of 1993. That year too many devotees climbed aboard the pagoda and it sank, and about 300 people are said to have died. The procession was scaled down afterward, and a large pagoda returned to the festival in 2014. Since then the festival has also served as a memorial: it is reported that a Mass for the victims is held aboard a vessel moored over the spot where the original pagoda went down. During the COVID-19 pandemic the event was scaled back and the cross was carried on a government yacht.

For travelers, the festival is both a colorful spectacle and a living expression of local faith. In the morning, rites continue at the church; once the cross is carried to the riverbank and placed on the pagoda, the river procession begins. After the river procession, the cross is carried through the streets, and visitors have described costumed dance groups and street festivities along the way. The scale and schedule change a little every year, so check the latest announcements from the Bocaue municipal government, the parish and the Department of Tourism before you go.

The pagoda is a ceremonial barge topped with a multi-tiered decorated structure. It moves slowly down the Bocaue River with music playing, and accounts describe passengers sharing a generous spread of food. It is the most striking sight of the day, so claim a spot on the riverbank early.

blocks.title: Ligiran: the boats that surround the pagoda

children.text: The custom of small boats encircling and following the pagoda is called ligiran, a name said to come from a word meaning "to surround." Many small boats and motorboats move together, so the whole river becomes part of the procession.

The star of the festival is the wooden cross said to have been found in the river in 1850. It is enshrined at St. Martin of Tours Parish Church, where you can see devotees line up to touch or kiss it. This is a religious event, so mind your clothing and manners.

blocks.title: From the church to the riverbank

children.text: The cross is carried from the Spanish-era Bocaue Church to the riverbank, placed on the pagoda, and then carried through the streets again after the river procession. Visitors have reported that the devotees' procession continues into the night.

Since 2014, a Mass for the victims is reported to be held on a vessel moored over the spot where the first pagoda sank. It is a reminder that the festival is about remembrance and safety as well as celebration.

Visitors have described student dance groups in traditional and Muslim-style costumes and women in long dresses joining the street festivities. Firefighters also spray water from hoses, and children play in the spray.
A nine-day novena called the Lutina is held before the festival. Masses and prayers over those days, along with stalls and entertainment, gradually build the festive mood before the main day.
Stalls, fairs and performances are reported during the festival. You can find local snacks and meals around the venue, but check hygiene and prices yourself.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Leave in the morning and watch the river and street processions

children.text: Head north from Manila. On festival days the town center and main roads are congested, so an early start is best.
Arrive in Bocaue and walk around St. Martin of Tours Parish Church to take in the atmosphere where the cross is enshrined.
Move to the riverbank before the procession starts and find a spot with a good view. The schedule and order change every year, so follow local announcements and cordons.
Rest in the shade and have lunch between viewings. Midday is very hot and humid.
Watch the street procession carrying the cross and the dance performances.
Start heading home before the crowds leave all at once.
The schedule may vary from year to year. Bring a hat, water and a rain jacket, and agree on a meeting point with your group in advance.

items.title: Bulacan heritage towns combined
items.subtitle: Visit nearby churches and shrines before or after the festival

children.text: The day before or after the festival, visit the Obando shrine and Meycauayan Church.
Move on to Bocaue to see the church and the riverside.
Continue to Baliwag or Malolos to see churches and museums.
Combining Bulacan's churches makes a full day around the festival.

items.title: From Manila by bus or van

children.text: To reach Bocaue from Manila, take a bus, jeepney or van toward the NLEX corridor. A route-planning site lists a direct bus from Sulu in Manila to NLEX Marilao running about every
15 minutes
, with a fare of about
and a trip of about
2 hours

(an estimate for 2026 that varies with the starting point). Another guide (January 2026) lists buses from SM North and Trinoma to Bocaue at about ₱100 and vans at about ₱45, so fares can be lower from some terminals. Check actual times and fares locally.
From Caloocan and Valenzuela, buses and jeepneys along MacArthur Highway are reported to run to the Bocaue Public Market. The fare is about
(a route-planning site estimates ₱25~45 per segment; another guide gives ₱30~80 from Cubao and Monumento), and travel time varies widely with traffic.
Roads into town may be closed on festival days, so plan to get off at the edge of town and walk in.
The distance from Manila to Bocaue is about
depending on the starting point, and the drive is reported to take about
30 minutes
in normal conditions, but on festival days it can take several times longer.
Parking near the venue is difficult. Park on the outskirts and walk in.
App-based taxis such as Grab can be hard to book on festival days, so arrange your trip home in advance.
The church and the riverbank are within walking distance of each other. Tricycles may be restricted on festival days.
Within town, follow local announcements and cordons.
The festival is centered on the first Sunday of July. The Tourism Promotions Board (TPB) has listed
July 4–7

, but dates change from year to year, so confirm before you go. July is the rainy season in the Philippines, and days are hot and humid. If it rains, the river procession schedule may change, so bring a rain jacket and a waterproof bag.

A sensible plan is to arrive early and take in the church and the riverbank, rest indoors or in the shade at midday, and come back out for the afternoon street procession. Accommodation and transport get crowded around the event, so move early. For photos, watch the pagoda on the river at least once, either in the morning or the afternoon, and spend the rest of the time at the church plaza and the street procession so you capture both scenes. The streets get dark after sunset and the crowds head home at once, so plan to leave before dark.

items.label: Accommodation
items.note: Options in Bocaue are limited, so many people stay in Manila and make a day trip

and may vary with local conditions.

Bocaue is close to Manila, so most visitors stay in Manila or a nearby city and come as a day trip. Rooms in nearby cities fill up early around the festival, so book once the dates are set. Check exact room prices and availability by date on a booking site.

Food centers on street stalls and restaurants around the market. Bulacan is known in the Philippines for its sweets and snacks, and you can reportedly try local treats at nearby markets. Check hygiene at street stalls and drink plenty of water. Accounts describe people aboard the pagoda sharing a generous spread of food, but boarding the pagoda is limited under safety rules.
Procession times and routes change every year, so check the latest announcements from the municipal government and the parish.
Arrive early and claim a spot on the riverbank or in front of the church; it makes photography much easier.
July is the rainy season, so bring a rain jacket and a waterproof bag, and wrap your electronics in plastic.
You may get wet where firefighters spray water, so bring a change of clothes.
This is a religious event, so avoid sleeveless tops and short pants and behave respectfully around the cross and sacred images.
Keep your phone and wallet in front of you and split your cash.
Agree on a meeting point in case you get separated; mobile signal may be unreliable.
The number of people allowed aboard the pagoda is limited for safety. Follow the instructions of the marshals.
About 300 people died here in the 1993 pagoda sinking. Only the permitted number of people should board any boat on the river, and you must follow life jacket rules and the marshals' instructions.
Roads are closed and crowds are very large on event days. Watch for pickpockets and keep valuables in front of you.
In the July rainy season, sudden showers and changes in river level are possible. The schedule may change or be canceled.
When taking photos by the river, stay away from slippery banks and the water's edge.
This is a religious event, so avoid loud noise and disrespectful photography during rites.
Event schedules and rules change from year to year, so check official announcements right before your visit.
A shrine in Obando, a short distance south of Bocaue. It is known for a May fertility rite, and you can visit the church at other times too.
A historic Bulacan town to the south of Bocaue where you can see the church and living heritage together.
The cathedral in Malolos, the capital of Bulacan. It makes a good stop on the way north from Bocaue.
Baliwag, in northern Bulacan, offers churches, museums and traditional craft.
